A Multi-Stage Dockerfile

Why generating the Prisma client needs devDependencies, and npm prune's trick for keeping the generated client while still shipping a lean image.

The API's first Dockerfile — Weeks 1–5 only ever containerized infrastructure (MySQL, Mailpit), never the app itself, precisely because a fast host-side edit/reload loop matters more while it's under active development than a production-shaped image does. Week 6 is where that stops being true: there's now a worker process to run alongside the API, and that's the natural point to show what running this "for real" looks like.

# Figure 6.19: Dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
COPY prisma ./prisma
RUN npm ci

FROM node:22-alpine AS production
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
RUN npm prune --omit=dev

COPY prisma ./prisma
COPY src ./src

USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]

Two stages, for a reason specific to Prisma: package.json's postinstall script runs prisma generate, which needs the prisma CLI — a devDependency — and prisma/schema.prisma to generate a client against. A plain npm ci --omit=dev in one stage would skip installing prisma entirely, and postinstall would fail. The deps stage runs a full npm ci (every dependency) purely to produce a node_modules with the generated client sitting inside it; the production stage copies that whole node_modules over, then npm prune --omit=dev strips out everything listed under devDependencies (prisma, jest, supertest, ...) — leaving the runtime dependency @prisma/client and the query engine prisma generate already produced untouched, since neither is itself a devDependency being pruned. The result: a final image with the same dev-dependency-free node_modules a plain npm ci --omit=dev would give, without ever needing the prisma CLI present in the stage that actually ships.
